newsitem.title: INDIA: India seeks foreign funds for airports, air safety.
newsitem.headline: India seeks foreign funds for airports, air safety.

text.p: India needs huge doses of private investment to build vital airport infrastructure and spruce up flight safety, aviation experts said on Friday.

"If money is required for air safety, then the government has to provide it. If they cannot, let them privatise," Hamid Shahul, former chairman of the state-run Airports Authority of India, told a seminar on flight safety in New Delhi.

"India would need an investment of at least 200 billion rupees ($558 million) if it wants to ensure the minimum safety standards for its airports and air corridors," said V.K. Mathur, another former chief of the Airports Authority.

Flight safety concerns resurfaced in India in December, when a Saudi Arabia Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakh Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 freighter collided near Delhi in the world's worst mid-air collision, killing all 349 people on board.
India needed to update its outdated radar system, Shahul said.
"The only way those funds can come is through foreign investment, so let us make the environment congenial for foreign investors," Mathur said.
Indian aviation officials say a multi-million-dollar plan to modernise radar and communications systems at major airports has fallen well behind schedule.
A state-of-the-art air traffic control system built by U.S. Raytheon Company has been held up by technical problems. Raytheon said last November that it would be ready for use soon.
India dismantled a state aviation monopoly as part of a series of sweeping economic reforms in 1991, opening its skies to a dozen private airlines.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's cabinet earlier this month allowed foreign investors to take stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines but said foreign airlines cannot directly buy stakes in domestic airlines.

Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim was quoted by Business Standard newspaper on Friday as saying that the government would encourage foreign investors, even airlines, to invest in upgrading Indian airports.
"Here there is confusion. I have asked the civil aviation secretary to clarify this," he said.
India has five international and 87 domestic airports. The Delhi and Bombay airports handle nearly half the total traffic.

S.S. Sidhu, an aviation analyst, said both the airline and airport businesses were highly capital-intensive and added that governments in developing countries found it difficult to fund their modernisation.
"The equipment at Delhi and Bombay airports are capable of handling a maximum of 12 flights per hour but during the peak hours they have to handle as many as 28 planes," Sidhu said.
Indian airports handled 23 million passengers in the year 1993/94 and that figure is estimated to rise to 110 million by the year 2011.
"If we don't wake up to the challenge now, we might end up losing our credibility in the global market," Sidhu said.
